description:
Designing a space mission requires balancing mission goals, spacecraft design, scientific tools, launch vehicles, budgets, power, mass, communication, and orbital limits.

Your task is to create an interactive game where students design, manage, and simulate a complete space mission, making engineering decisions and managing limited resources while discovering how each choice affects mission success.
summary:
Rewind Earth is a browser application that links two things students normally meet separately: designing a satellite, and living with what it can see.

In the first mode you build an Earth-observing satellite in 3D — camera, solar wings, antenna, battery, propulsion and orbit altitude — while live mass, power, data-return and cost budgets react to every choice and the model physically changes shape. You launch it, then get a scored debrief explaining every budget you missed.

In the second, the Earth Atlas, you compare any two dates of NASA GIBS imagery on one map with a swipe, play the years forward, and measure the change. In our measurement frame the Aral Sea’s water surface fell from 2,885 km² to 843 km² between 20 August 2000 and 20 August 2024 — about 71%.

The modes connect: the camera you chose sets how closely you may then examine the real archive. That is the challenge’s central trade-off made tangible — a wide camera revisits daily but loses a shoreline inside its pixels; a sharp one resolves it, yet returns rarely and cannot downlink what it gathers.

It matters because satellite design decides which planetary changes we can detect at all.
